chunks: "A reflection happens anywhere the impedance the wave sees changes. So I'd split the causes into two groups. The first is the terminations.
If the source or the load isn't equal to Z 0 , you get a reflection at that end.
A CMOS receiver is nearly an open circuit, and a driver might be 10 ohms or 40, so the typical unterminated net has mismatches at both ends.
The second group is everything in between that changes the local inductance or capacitance per unit length. Vias add pad capacitance and barrel inductance.
A stub or a T-junction hangs an extra length of line, which looks like capacitance or splits the impedance in half. Connectors and package leads have their own geometry.
A trace that changes width, layer, or dielectric changes its characteristic impedance, and a gap or split in the reference plane forces the return current to detour and adds inductance.
Even the pad of a component, an ESD diode or a test point adds a picofarad or so. Fabrication tolerance means a nominal 50 ohm line is only 50 ohms plus or minus about 10 percent.
Whether they matter depends on size: a 1 picofarads pad is fine for a 10 megahertz clock and a serious reflection at 100 picosecond edges.
I'd minimise them in layout and use a TDR to find the ones that remain."
